0 · The real problem: a model must remain useful after a policy starts exploiting it

A world model is a learned predictor of the consequences of interventions. Its engineering objective is to reduce the cost of acquiring a competent policy: fewer physical trials, less expensive environment interaction, faster planning, or better transfer to new tasks. Its scientific difficulty is that the distribution on which a model is tested is chosen by a decision maker that is optimizing against that very model. A planner actively searches for exceptional trajectories. Those can be exceptional because they are good, or because the simulator is wrong.

This distinction organizes the entire field. A next-frame model is trained to explain recorded transitions. A control model must answer a counterfactual: “If I apply this action, what will happen?” A reusable simulator must answer many such questions across objects, contexts, and goals. A policy-learning simulator must answer them millions of times cheaply enough to make synthetic experience worthwhile. These are related objectives with different failure modes; the word “world” does not erase their differences.

The thesis: the research progression is a sequence of compromises over what to preserve, how to represent uncertainty, and where to spend computation. PILCO and PETS preserve uncertainty over physical dynamics. PlaNet and Dreamer preserve a predictive latent state and move control into it. MuZero and TD-MPC preserve decision-relevant quantities. IRIS and DIAMOND restore detailed observations. Genie learns interactive latent controls from passive videos. V-JEPA 2 and Dreamer 4 reconnect video-scale learning to grounded intervention and policy improvement. Understanding the compromise explains more than memorizing a list of architectures.

How to read this guide

First read §§1–3 to establish the statistical problem and the model-use choices. Then follow the chronological families in §§4–11; each landmark is explained through its learning objective, deployment algorithm, original figures, and the problem left for its successors. The last sections examine error, computational cost, and evidence. Prerequisites are probability, gradient descent, basic reinforcement learning, and attention. Definitions are introduced where they become necessary.

The paper images below are crops of the original PDFs, with source and local-PDF links. They are not decorative examples: the surrounding text explains what the arrows, axes, and comparisons establish. Dates follow first reports where practical; experiments refer to the linked versions. This is a research curriculum, not a claim that every published world-model variant has been reproduced or ranked.

1 · The mathematical contract: what is being predicted, for whom?

1.1 Hidden state, observation, and a sufficient history

Write the environment as a partially observed controlled process. The physical state x_t can include object velocity, friction, contact mode, and an occluded object's location. Observation o_t is what the camera or sensors report. Action a_t has units, a coordinate frame, a control frequency, and a delay. The learned state s_t is a statistic of the history, not necessarily an estimate of every physical variable.

xt+1∼P(x′∣xt,at),ot∼O(o∣xt),Ht=(o0,a0,…,at−1,ot),bt(x)=P(xt=x∣Ht),st=eθ(Ht),World model:P^θ(st+1,rt,ct∣st,at),Policy:at∼π(a∣st,goal),J(π)=E ⁣[∑tγtrt]subject to interaction/compute constraints.\begin{aligned}x_{t+1}&\sim P(x'\mid x_t,a_t),\quad o_t\sim O(o\mid x_t),\\H_t&=(o_0,a_0,\ldots,a_{t-1},o_t),\\b_t(x)&=P(x_t=x\mid H_t),\quad s_t=e_\theta(H_t),\\\text{World model:}\quad&\hat P_\theta(s_{t+1},r_t,c_t\mid s_t,a_t),\\\text{Policy:}\quad&a_t\sim\pi(a\mid s_t,\mathrm{goal}),\\J(\pi)&=\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_t\gamma^tr_t\right]\quad\text{subject to interaction/compute constraints}.\end{aligned}xt+1​Ht​bt​(x)World model:Policy:J(π)​∼P(x′∣xt​,at​),ot​∼O(o∣xt​),=(o0​,a0​,…,at−1​,ot​),=P(xt​=x∣Ht​),st​=eθ​(Ht​),P^θ​(st+1​,rt​,ct​∣st​,at​),at​∼π(a∣st​,goal),=E[t∑​γtrt​]subject to interaction/compute constraints.​

Here c_t is continuation, so a predicted failure or terminal event can stop future reward. A reward predictor without a termination model may give value to steps that cannot occur. Likewise a model that predicts a sequence without a calibrated action convention may be a useful video generator but cannot yet act as the transition function of a robot controller.

Two pictures can be identical while their optimal actions differ: a ball at the same position can be moving left or right; a gripper can touch a box lightly or already support its weight. Recurrence and history are attempts to infer the hidden distinction. A learned latent is sufficient for a task when the future quantities required for choosing actions depend on history only through that latent. This is a property to evaluate, not a consequence of calling a network an RSSM or a Transformer.

Derivation: why the predictive state is a belief, not the latest frame

Assumptions and notation. Let sₜ be a hidden Markov state, aₜ a chosen action, oₜ an observation, T(s′|s,a) the transition distribution, and O(o|s) the observation likelihood. The complete history is hₜ=(o₀,a₀,…,oₜ). For this derivation, the model is known and observations are conditionally independent given the current state. Write bₜ(s)=P(sₜ=s|hₜ). Sums below become integrals for continuous states.

  1. Predict using the action. Marginalize the old hidden state: b̄ₜ₊₁(s′)=ΣₛT(s′|s,aₜ)bₜ(s). This is the law of total probability, not a point prediction.
  2. Correct using the observation. Bayes' rule multiplies the predicted probability by how likely the new observation is under each candidate state.
  3. Normalize. The denominator is the probability of the observation under the predictive mixture; it makes the updated belief sum to one.
bt+1(s′)=O(ot+1∣s′)∑sT(s′∣s,at)bt(s)∑uO(ot+1∣u)∑sT(u∣s,at)bt(s),P(ot+1∣ht,at)=∑s′O(ot+1∣s′)bˉt+1(s′).\begin{aligned}b_{t+1}(s')&=\frac{O(o_{t+1}\mid s')\sum_sT(s'\mid s,a_t)b_t(s)}{\sum_uO(o_{t+1}\mid u)\sum_sT(u\mid s,a_t)b_t(s)},\\P(o_{t+1}\mid h_t,a_t)&=\sum_{s'}O(o_{t+1}\mid s')\bar b_{t+1}(s').\end{aligned}bt+1​(s′)P(ot+1​∣ht​,at​)​=∑u​O(ot+1​∣u)∑s​T(u∣s,at​)bt​(s)O(ot+1​∣s′)∑s​T(s′∣s,at​)bt​(s)​,=s′∑​O(ot+1​∣s′)bˉt+1​(s′).​

The Markov and observation assumptions imply that this belief contains everything in the history required to predict future observations and rewards under future actions. Thus a partially observed problem becomes a fully observed problem whose state is a probability distribution. A deterministic recurrent vector can encode such a distribution implicitly; being deterministic as a function of history does not mean the physical future is deterministic.

What an RSSM approximates. Its recurrent state and stochastic posterior approximate a useful history summary and uncertainty distribution. The ELBO does not prove that this summary is a sufficient belief, and latent coordinates need not correspond to physical variables. If two physically different situations produce identical histories, no encoder can uniquely distinguish them without another informative observation or intervention.

Exercise — Update a belief about hidden friction

A surface is high-friction with prior probability 0.6 and low-friction with probability 0.4. A probe reports “little slip” with probabilities 0.9 and 0.2 respectively. The probe does not change the friction. Compute the posterior, and explain why replacing it by the most likely friction can lose useful information.

Show worked solution

The joint probabilities of high friction and the report, and low friction and the report, are 0.6×0.9=0.54 and 0.4×0.2=0.08. The report probability is 0.62, so:

P(high∣little slip)=0.540.62≈0.8710,P(low∣little slip)=0.080.62≈0.1290.\begin{aligned}P(\mathrm{high}\mid\text{little slip})&=\frac{0.54}{0.62}\approx0.8710,\\P(\mathrm{low}\mid\text{little slip})&=\frac{0.08}{0.62}\approx0.1290.\end{aligned}P(high∣little slip)P(low∣little slip)​=0.620.54​≈0.8710,=0.620.08​≈0.1290.​

A maximum-probability state estimate chooses high friction and discards the remaining 12.9% probability. If slipping causes a large loss, that tail can change the optimal action. An expected-cost or risk-sensitive controller can use the distribution, whereas a plug-in estimate requires an additional approximation. This conclusion concerns the stated calibrated likelihoods; an inaccurate sensor model can make the numerical posterior misleading.

1.2 Four different models that are often conflated

Model targetWhat its loss encouragesWhat can consume itWhat may be discarded
Physical state transitionPredict positions, velocities, forcesMPC, policy optimization, uncertainty propagationVisual appearance absent from the state
Observation-generating latent dynamicsExplain future observations and rewardsImagined actor learning; rendered simulatorDetails removed by the encoder/tokenizer
Value-oriented latent dynamicsPreserve rewards, values, or useful Bellman updatesSearch or short-horizon planningVisually real facts irrelevant to training objectives
Predictive embedding dynamicsMatch future encoder featuresGoal-reaching energy, representation-based planningFeatures to which the encoder is invariant

A smaller representation can improve sample efficiency by ignoring nuisance variables. The same invariance can destroy information required by a different goal. If two cups have different masses but look identical, a vision-only model may correctly represent visual equivalence while failing at force-sensitive lifting. Conversely, accurately reconstructing wallpaper consumes model capacity without improving a tabletop controller. Representation selection is an allocation of finite information capacity.

1.3 Distributional uncertainty has more than one meaning

A probabilistic output models ambiguity conditional on the available state: process noise, hidden information, or multiple plausible futures. This is aleatoric uncertainty relative to the chosen observation model. Epistemic uncertainty concerns uncertainty about the dynamics function itself. A network that predicts a broad Gaussian is not automatically aware that its input is outside the dataset. Ensembles approximate the second quantity by disagreement, but shared training data and inductive biases can make every member confidently wrong.

For an ensemble of Gaussian predictors with means μ_b and covariances Σ_b, the law of total variance gives a useful diagnostic decomposition:

μˉ=1B∑bμb,Var⁡(next state)≈1B∑bΣb⏟within-model noise+1B∑b(μb−μˉ)(μb−μˉ)⊤⏟between-model disagreement.\begin{aligned}\bar\mu&=\frac1B\sum_b\mu_b,\\\operatorname{Var}(\text{next state})&\approx\underbrace{\frac1B\sum_b\Sigma_b}_{\text{within-model noise}}+\underbrace{\frac1B\sum_b(\mu_b-\bar\mu)(\mu_b-\bar\mu)^\top}_{\text{between-model disagreement}}.\end{aligned}μˉ​Var(next state)​=B1​b∑​μb​,≈within-model noiseB1​b∑​Σb​​​+between-model disagreementB1​b∑​(μb​−μˉ​)(μb​−μˉ​)⊤​​.​

This decomposition is exact for the specified mixture. Interpreting its terms as true environmental versus epistemic uncertainty is a modeling assumption. Increasing data may reduce ensemble disagreement without fixing a systematically incorrect contact model. The distinction matters when a planner treats uncertainty as a cost, a reason to gather data, or a distribution over acceptable risk. [3]

2 · A chronological map: the objective changes before the architecture does

The oldest lineage learns dynamics because real experiments are expensive. PILCO (2011) emphasizes uncertainty propagation. PETS (2018) asks whether expressive neural models can retain that data efficiency. World Models (2018) separates visual compression, recurrent prediction, and control. PlaNet (2018/2019) makes latent planning directly from images competitive. These contributions establish the components of the modern imagination loop. [1] [3] [2] [4]

The 2019 split is decisive. Dreamer learns an actor and critic in latent imagination; MuZero learns a latent model tailored to search. MBPO asks how much synthetic rollout can safely be trusted. The next wave improves the foundations: DreamerV2/V3, EfficientZero, and TD-MPC/TD-MPC2 solve categorical representation, optimization stability, limited-data search, and continuous-control scale. These are different responses to the same reality: a model error is important in proportion to how it changes decisions. [5] [9] [11] [6] [7] [10] [14]

From 2022 onward, powerful sequence generators reopen the question of observation fidelity. IRIS uses visual tokens; DIAMOND uses diffusion; Genie discovers latent actions in video. In parallel, action-free pretraining, predictive embeddings, and video foundation platforms broaden the data source. Dreamer 4 combines a scalable generative model with offline policy improvement. The field therefore has overlapping branches, not a linear succession in which a video model makes task-oriented MPC obsolete. [15] [16] [17] [23] [20] [8]

Landmark changeBottleneck being addressedCharacteristic descendants or neighboring variants
PILCO → PETSAccurate learning from few costly trialsProbabilistic ensembles, trajectory sampling, uncertainty-aware MPC
PlaNet → DreamerPixel-space planning cost and long-horizon creditDreamerV2/V3, Plan2Explore, DayDreamer, HarmonyDream, STORM
MuZero → EfficientZeroLearn only what search requires; then reduce data demandsConsistency learning, value-prefix targets, corrected replay targets
TD-MPC → TD-MPC2Continuous actions and stable multi-task scalingActor-guided trajectory optimization, normalized latent/value learning
IRIS → DIAMONDGenerative details lost by compact abstractionsToken sequence simulators versus diffusion observation simulators
Genie / APV → V-JEPA 2 / Dreamer 4Connect abundant passive video to interventionsLatent-action discovery, action-conditioned post-training, offline imagination

3 · Era I: uncertainty-aware dynamics and selective imagination

3.1 PILCO: analytic uncertainty propagation buys data efficiency

PILCO fits Gaussian-process dynamics to observed state-action transitions. The GP supplies a predictive distribution that incorporates uncertainty from limited data. Rather than replacing the next state by its mean and repeatedly applying a deterministic model, PILCO approximately propagates a state distribution through the dynamics and policy. Expected cumulative cost can then be differentiated with respect to policy parameters. [1]

The key insight is that a policy trained against only the mean transition can seek regions where the estimated model is conveniently optimistic. Propagating uncertainty changes expected cost even if mean predictions are unchanged. For a nonlinear cost, E[c(x)]\mathbb E[c(x)]E[c(x)] generally differs from c(E[x])c(\mathbb E[x])c(E[x]); the variance of a predicted trajectory is part of policy evaluation. Moment matching makes the calculation tractable, but a Gaussian approximation can hide multimodal outcomes such as “object sticks” versus “object slips.” Sparse data and low-dimensional states are PILCO's natural regime; large raw images and complex contact dynamics stress both GP scaling and distributional approximations.

3.2 PETS: probabilistic ensembles plus trajectory sampling

PETS replaces GP dynamics with an ensemble of probabilistic neural networks. Each network predicts a distribution, typically Gaussian, over a state change; different bootstrap datasets produce distinct models. For one network, Gaussian negative log likelihood includes a variance-weighted residual and a log-determinant penalty. The residual discourages inaccurate means, while the determinant prevents explaining every error by infinite predicted variance. [3]

Δx∼N(μθ(x,a),Σθ(x,a)),LNLL=12(Δx−μ)⊤Σ−1(Δx−μ)+12log⁡det⁡Σ+constant,A=(at,…,at+H−1),J^(A)=1P∑p=1P∑hγhr(xh(p),ah).\begin{aligned}\Delta x&\sim\mathcal N(\mu_\theta(x,a),\Sigma_\theta(x,a)),\\\mathcal L_{\mathrm{NLL}}&=\tfrac12(\Delta x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\Delta x-\mu)+\tfrac12\log\det\Sigma+\mathrm{constant},\\A&=(a_t,\ldots,a_{t+H-1}),\\\hat J(A)&=\frac1P\sum_{p=1}^P\sum_h\gamma^h r(x_h^{(p)},a_h).\end{aligned}ΔxLNLL​AJ^(A)​∼N(μθ​(x,a),Σθ​(x,a)),=21​(Δx−μ)⊤Σ−1(Δx−μ)+21​logdetΣ+constant,=(at​,…,at+H−1​),=P1​p=1∑P​h∑​γhr(xh(p)​,ah​).​

Read the original Figure 1 left to right. The model panel contains alternative fitted functions and their uncertainty bands. The middle panel shows how particles sample possible future states. The right panel shows many imagined trajectories being used to choose an action sequence. The planner is integrating over modeled uncertainty; it is not simply selecting the trajectory with the highest possible outcome. The picture also separates the learned model from the optimizer, which is useful when diagnosing an implementation: poor control can come from either inaccurate predictions or insufficient search.

Trajectory-sampling variants determine when each particle selects an ensemble member. Resampling a member at every time step blends model uncertainty differently from fixing its identity throughout a trajectory. The fixed-member variant preserves a coherent dynamics hypothesis over time, making long-range disagreement interpretable. Moment matching, by comparison, collapses a potentially multimodal distribution into a convenient parametric approximation. PETS experimentally separates the choice of dynamics model from the method of propagating its uncertainty.

The cross-entropy method (CEM) optimizes actions by sampling sequences from a Gaussian, retaining an elite fraction, and refitting the mean and variance to those elites. MPC executes the first action and replans from the next real state. CEM here is an optimization procedure; it is unrelated to the categorical cross-entropy loss used for training neural classifiers. Warm-starting the next planning distribution with the previous plan shifted by one step saves computation and encourages temporal consistency.

Derivation: separate uncertainty sources and preserve their time correlations

Let M identify an ensemble member and Y its predicted next-state coordinate. Assume member m predicts mean μₘ and variance σ²ₘ, and use a uniform distribution over members as an approximation to model uncertainty. The following identity is exact for the resulting mixture even when that mixture is not a Gaussian.

Y−E[Y]=(Y−E[Y∣M])+(E[Y∣M]−E[Y]),Var⁡(Y)=E[(Y−E[Y∣M])2]+E[(E[Y∣M]−E[Y])2]+2E[(Y−E[Y∣M])(E[Y∣M]−E[Y])]=EM[σM2]+Var⁡M(μM).\begin{aligned}Y-\mathbb E[Y]&=(Y-\mathbb E[Y\mid M])+(\mathbb E[Y\mid M]-\mathbb E[Y]),\\\operatorname{Var}(Y)&=\mathbb E[(Y-\mathbb E[Y\mid M])^2]\\&\quad+\mathbb E[(\mathbb E[Y\mid M]-\mathbb E[Y])^2]\\&\quad+2\mathbb E[(Y-\mathbb E[Y\mid M])(\mathbb E[Y\mid M]-\mathbb E[Y])]\\&=\mathbb E_M[\sigma_M^2]+\operatorname{Var}_M(\mu_M).\end{aligned}Y−E[Y]Var(Y)​=(Y−E[Y∣M])+(E[Y∣M]−E[Y]),=E[(Y−E[Y∣M])2]+E[(E[Y∣M]−E[Y])2]+2E[(Y−E[Y∣M])(E[Y∣M]−E[Y])]=EM​[σM2​]+VarM​(μM​).​

The cross term vanishes because E[Y−E[Y|M]|M]=0; conditioning on M turns its other factor into a constant. The first term is within-model variability, commonly used to represent aleatoric uncertainty. The second is disagreement about the mean, commonly used as an epistemic proxy. Two equally weighted members with means −1 and +1 and variance 0.25 each give total variance 0.25+1=1.25. Using only the ensemble mean would predict zero and erase both the modes and their spread.

Why a trajectory sampler must decide when to resample the member. Consider dynamics sₜ₊₁=sₜ+m with an unknown but time-invariant m∈{−1,+1}. Holding one sampled m for an H-step particle produces sH=s₀±H, with variance H². Independently resampling m at every step produces a random walk with variance H. These are different stochastic processes despite identical one-step marginals. PETS' trajectory-sampling variants expose this distinction: uncertainty about a fixed dynamics parameter should not automatically be treated as fresh process noise.

The decomposition does not certify ensemble calibration. Members trained on similar data can agree on the same wrong extrapolation, making the epistemic proxy small exactly where the model is inaccurate. One must also decide whether uncertainty penalizes an action, encourages exploration, or is simply integrated out during planning.

3.3 MBPO and MOPO: more synthetic data is not automatically better

MBPO branches short model rollouts from real replay states and mixes the resulting transitions with real data for policy learning. This limits the distance over which errors can accumulate and anchors the synthetic state distribution to observed data. It separates two quantities that are easily confused: the amount of imagined data and the length of each imagined trajectory. Many short, well-anchored rollouts can be preferable to a few long, drifting ones. [11]

MOPO addresses the offline setting, where collecting corrective real transitions is unavailable. It modifies the reward with a penalty based on model uncertainty, schematically r~=r^−λu\tilde r=\hat r-\lambda ur~=r^−λu. This discourages policies from exploiting unsupported transitions. The guarantee in such analyses depends on uncertainty controlling model error in a suitable sense; a convenient neural variance is not automatically a valid bound. Excessive pessimism can also suppress necessary exploration-like action sequences even when they exist in the dataset. [12]

These methods expose a lasting tradeoff. Longer model rollouts reduce dependence on an imperfect value bootstrap but increase dynamics bias. Shorter rollouts contain less transition error but rely more on a learned critic. “Trust the model for H steps” is a statistical decision. It should depend on state, action, and data coverage, although many practical algorithms use one global horizon for efficiency.

4 · Era II-A: PlaNet makes latent dynamics usable for control

4.1 Why a deterministic RNN or a purely stochastic state is insufficient

A deterministic recurrent network has memory but must compress all unresolved futures into one representation and output rule. A purely stochastic state-space model can represent uncertainty but struggles to retain stable information over long sequences. PlaNet's recurrent state-space model (RSSM) combines a deterministic recurrent path h_t with a stochastic state z_t. The current observation informs the posterior; the transition prior predicts the stochastic state when the observation is unavailable. [4]

In original Figure 2, squares are deterministic quantities and circles are stochastic variables. Solid edges specify the generative process; dashed edges specify inference. In the RSSM panel, information can travel along the deterministic h path without being resampled at each step, while z represents uncertain state information. The shaded observed steps show the posterior correcting the model. The final unobserved step must use the prior. That last distinction is precisely the difference between reconstructing a replay sequence and simulating a future.

ht=fθ(ht−1,zt−1,at−1),qϕ(zt∣ht,ot)posterior: current evidence,pθ(zt∣ht)prior: imagination,pθ(ot,rt∣ht,zt)observation/reward predictions.\begin{aligned}h_t&=f_\theta(h_{t-1},z_{t-1},a_{t-1}),\\q_\phi(z_t\mid h_t,o_t)&\quad\text{posterior: current evidence},\\p_\theta(z_t\mid h_t)&\quad\text{prior: imagination},\\p_\theta(o_t,r_t\mid h_t,z_t)&\quad\text{observation/reward predictions}.\end{aligned}ht​qϕ​(zt​∣ht​,ot​)pθ​(zt​∣ht​)pθ​(ot​,rt​∣ht​,zt​)​=fθ​(ht−1​,zt−1​,at−1​),posterior: current evidence,prior: imagination,observation/reward predictions.​

A model can reconstruct sharply while its prior is poor: the posterior simply supplies information from each new image that the transition model could never have predicted. Therefore “the autoencoder looks good” is not a world-model validation. A useful test conditions on a short real prefix, switches to prior-only rollout under recorded actions, and evaluates the free-running prediction. Even that test must later be supplemented by novel-action and closed-loop control tests.

4.2 Deriving the sequential variational objective

For a controlled latent model, introduce an approximate filtering posterior q(z_1:T | o_1:T,a_1:T). Insert q/qq/qq/q inside the marginal likelihood integral and apply Jensen's inequality. The resulting evidence lower bound contains expected reconstruction likelihood and a divergence from the dynamics prior. For the RSSM, with h determined by the preceding latent/action history:

log⁡p(o1:T,r1:T∣a<T)≥∑tEq[log⁡p(ot∣ht,zt)+log⁡p(rt∣ht,zt)]−∑tEq[DKL(q(zt∣ht,ot)∥p(zt∣ht))].Minimize the negative bound; optionally reweight KL.\begin{aligned}\log p(o_{1:T},r_{1:T}\mid a_{<T})&\ge\sum_t\mathbb E_q[\log p(o_t\mid h_t,z_t)+\log p(r_t\mid h_t,z_t)]\\&\quad-\sum_t\mathbb E_q[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(z_t\mid h_t,o_t)\|p(z_t\mid h_t))].\\&\text{Minimize the negative bound; optionally reweight KL.}\end{aligned}logp(o1:T​,r1:T​∣a<T​)​≥t∑​Eq​[logp(ot​∣ht​,zt​)+logp(rt​∣ht​,zt​)]−t∑​Eq​[DKL​(q(zt​∣ht​,ot​)∥p(zt​∣ht​))].Minimize the negative bound; optionally reweight KL.​

The reconstruction terms make state informative. The KL limits how much observation-specific information is injected beyond what the dynamics could predict. A strong KL may erase small but crucial features; a weak KL can create excellent posterior states that are unreachable from the imagined prior. The regularizer is therefore a rate–predictability tradeoff, not merely a conventional VAE term copied into a sequence model.

The deterministic path must not provide an unrestricted shortcut from the current image to its reconstruction. Otherwise the decoder can ignore the stochastic state and the carefully regularized dynamics cease to constrain the information used for prediction. Model diagrams are valuable precisely because they reveal such paths; names such as “variational” do not ensure that an implementation has preserved the intended bottleneck.

Derivation: every term in the RSSM evidence lower bound

Notation. Treat actions a as fixed conditioning information, set xₜ=(oₜ,rₜ), and let hₜ=f(hₜ₋₁,zₜ₋₁,aₜ₋₁) be deterministic. Assume p(x,z|a)=∏ₜp(zₜ|hₜ)p(xₜ|hₜ,zₜ), and choose a filtering variational family q(z|x,a)=∏ₜq(zₜ|hₜ,oₜ). For the expectation identity below, assume q is positive wherever the joint density p(x,z|a) is positive and the required integrals exist; finite KL also requires compatible support in the other direction. Reward need not enter the posterior even though it enters the likelihood.

  1. Insert a distribution without changing the integral. Multiply and divide by q to express the marginal likelihood as an expectation.
  2. Apply concavity of log. Jensen gives log E[Z]≥E[log Z]. This is the sole inequality in the basic derivation.
  3. Factor over time. Expand log p−log q using the causal products. Group each prior/posterior ratio into a conditional KL, with the earlier latent history still averaged under q.
log⁡p(x∣a)=log⁡∫q(z∣x,a)p(x,z∣a)q(z∣x,a) dz≥Eq[log⁡p(x,z∣a)−log⁡q(z∣x,a)]≡L,L=∑tEq[log⁡p(xt∣ht,zt)]−∑tEq(z<t)[DKL(q(zt∣ht,ot)∥p(zt∣ht))],log⁡p(x∣a)−L=DKL(q(z∣x,a)∥p(z∣x,a))≥0.\begin{aligned}\log p(x\mid a)&=\log\int q(z\mid x,a)\frac{p(x,z\mid a)}{q(z\mid x,a)}\,dz\\&\ge\mathbb E_q[\log p(x,z\mid a)-\log q(z\mid x,a)]\equiv\mathcal L,\\\mathcal L&=\sum_t\mathbb E_q[\log p(x_t\mid h_t,z_t)]\\&\quad-\sum_t\mathbb E_{q(z_{<t})}[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(z_t\mid h_t,o_t)\|p(z_t\mid h_t))],\\\log p(x\mid a)-\mathcal L&=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(z\mid x,a)\|p(z\mid x,a))\ge0.\end{aligned}logp(x∣a)Llogp(x∣a)−L​=log∫q(z∣x,a)q(z∣x,a)p(x,z∣a)​dz≥Eq​[logp(x,z∣a)−logq(z∣x,a)]≡L,=t∑​Eq​[logp(xt​∣ht​,zt​)]−t∑​Eq(z<t​)​[DKL​(q(zt​∣ht​,ot​)∥p(zt​∣ht​))],=DKL​(q(z∣x,a)∥p(z∣x,a))≥0.​

The exact posterior on the last line can depend on future observations even though q is restricted to filtering. Therefore the variational gap measures both imperfect parameters and the limitations of the chosen inference family. The observation and reward terms separate further only if their conditional likelihood factorizes. Gaussian likelihoods lead to weighted squared reconstruction errors; categorical likelihoods lead to cross-entropy. Changing likelihood variance changes the implicit weight of reconstruction.

Gradient reasoning. The posterior receives reconstruction gradients and regularization toward the prior. The prior learns to predict posterior information from history. KL balancing introduces stop-gradient operations to control those two learning signals separately; it is a modified gradient recipe, not an algebraic derivation of a new exact posterior. Replacing the KL coefficient by β also changes the optimization: β<1 does not generally preserve the lower-bound guarantee, while β≥1 lowers the ordinary bound further because KL is nonnegative.

Exercise — Compute a one-step variational bound

Take q(z)=N(1,0.25), p(z)=N(0,1), and E_q log p(x|z)=−2 nats. Compute KL(q||p), the ordinary ELBO, and the objective obtained with β=0.1. Is the latter automatically a lower bound on log p(x)?

Show worked solution

For one-dimensional Gaussians, use variance rather than standard deviation in the ratio:

DKL=12[σq2σp2+(μq−μp)2σp2−1+log⁡σp2σq2]=12[0.25+1−1+log⁡4]≈0.818147,L=−2−0.818147≈−2.818147  nats,Lβ=0.1=−2−0.0818147≈−2.081815  nats.\begin{aligned}D_{\mathrm{KL}}&=\frac12\left[\frac{\sigma_q^2}{\sigma_p^2}+\frac{(\mu_q-\mu_p)^2}{\sigma_p^2}-1+\log\frac{\sigma_p^2}{\sigma_q^2}\right]\\&=\tfrac12[0.25+1-1+\log4]\approx0.818147,\\\mathcal L&=-2-0.818147\approx-2.818147\;\mathrm{nats},\\\mathcal L_{\beta=0.1}&=-2-0.0818147\approx-2.081815\;\mathrm{nats}.\end{aligned}DKL​LLβ=0.1​​=21​[σp2​σq2​​+σp2​(μq​−μp​)2​−1+logσq2​σp2​​]=21​[0.25+1−1+log4]≈0.818147,=−2−0.818147≈−2.818147nats,=−2−0.0818147≈−2.081815nats.​

The smaller-β objective is larger, but Jensen justifies only the coefficient-one expression. The increase can exceed the variational gap, so it need not remain below the log evidence. Better numerical objective values across different β are not directly comparable likelihood bounds.

4.3 Latent overshooting and the difference between one-step and rollout supervision

Standard filtering training compares each one-step prior with a posterior informed by the next observation. It may never strongly penalize how a chain of several priors drifts. PlaNet's latent overshooting compares multi-step predictive distributions with inferred future states. It obtains a long-range learning signal without decoding a large image at every imagined step. [4]

Original Figure 3 makes the gradient paths visible. The first panel supervises adjacent transitions. Observation overshooting in the middle supervises longer rollouts through image likelihoods. Latent overshooting on the right supervises the state predictions themselves. A node labeled si∣js_{i\mid j}si∣j​ denotes a state at time i conditioned on observations through j: states with the same i but different j are different predictions of the same future. Their disagreement measures the gap that teacher forcing can conceal.

Do not infer that every descendant uses every PlaNet ingredient. The paper finds the benefit of overshooting depends on the model architecture; the RSSM itself carries strong long-range structure. Later methods change the loss, rollout scheme, or representation rather than mechanically retaining all components. A proper ablation asks whether the extra objective improves the chosen downstream controller, not whether the multi-step loss gets smaller.

PlaNet then plans with CEM in latent space, predicts rewards along candidate trajectories, executes one action, and updates the latent posterior with the next image. The costly decoder is needed for representation learning and visual inspection; it need not run for every candidate plan. This separation between a training decoder and deployment computation is one of the central computational advantages of latent control.

5 · Dreamer: amortize planning into an actor, then make the whole loop robust

5.1 Dreamer v1: value gradients through imagined trajectories

Dreamer retains latent dynamics but replaces per-action CEM search with actor–critic learning inside the model. Sample replay states, imagine trajectories by alternating the actor and transition prior, predict rewards, and train a value function. During real interaction, the actor selects an action from the current inferred state without a large trajectory search. Expensive reasoning has been amortized into policy parameters. [5]

Original Figure 3 separates three operations. Panel (a) fits dynamics from real experience; its observation pathway supplies information absent during prediction. Panel (b) has no future camera images: the actor and learned model generate a latent rollout and train behavior. Panel (c) uses the actor in the real environment, updating the inferred state as observations arrive. This figure prevents a common misunderstanding: the imagined actor is not trained by decoding thousands of videos and running a visual encoder over them. It can operate directly on compact latent states.

A truncated imagined return misses rewards beyond the model horizon. A learned critic supplies the terminal estimate. A λ-return smoothly combines bootstrap lengths:

Gtλ=r^t+γc^t[(1−λ)v^t+1+λGt+1λ],GHλ=v^H,Critic:regress toward stop_gradient⁡(Gtλ),Actor:increase expected Gtλ along imagined trajectories.\begin{aligned}G_t^\lambda&=\hat r_t+\gamma\hat c_t[(1-\lambda)\hat v_{t+1}+\lambda G_{t+1}^\lambda],\\G_H^\lambda&=\hat v_H,\\\text{Critic:}&\quad\text{regress toward }\operatorname{stop\_gradient}(G_t^\lambda),\\\text{Actor:}&\quad\text{increase expected }G_t^\lambda\text{ along imagined trajectories}.\end{aligned}Gtλ​GHλ​Critic:Actor:​=r^t​+γc^t​[(1−λ)v^t+1​+λGt+1λ​],=v^H​,regress toward stop_gradient(Gtλ​),increase expected Gtλ​ along imagined trajectories.​

The time index convention varies across implementations; the essential rule is that reward, continuation, and next-state value refer to the same transition. Bootstrapping reduces the required imagination horizon, while its errors become part of the objective. In continuous-action Dreamer v1, reparameterized action and latent samples permit gradients through the transition model and value predictions. The model's weights are held fixed during the behavior update, but differentiability through the model with respect to actions remains useful. “Frozen parameters” does not mean “block every input gradient.”

This pathwise gradient can be low variance, yet a smooth model can have the wrong derivative even when its predictions are reasonable. A contact threshold illustrates the problem: the true return can jump discontinuously while a learned differentiable model invents a gentle gradient. This motivates distinguishing prediction error, derivative error, and policy-gradient variance; they are different failure channels.

Derivation: λ-returns and gradients through an imagined control loop

For a finite imagined horizon H, use rewards rₜ on the transition from state sₜ to sₜ₊₁ and one fixed discount γ. Let V(s) be a learned terminal estimator. The n-step return includes n real or imagined rewards and one bootstrap. Define the truncated λ-mixture so its weights sum to one:

Gt(n)=∑j=0n−1γjrt+j+γnV(st+n),Gtλ=(1−λ)∑n=1H−t−1λn−1Gt(n)+λH−t−1Gt(H−t)=rt+γ[(1−λ)V(st+1)+λGt+1λ],GHλ=V(sH).\begin{aligned}G_t^{(n)}&=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\gamma^jr_{t+j}+\gamma^nV(s_{t+n}),\\G_t^\lambda&=(1-\lambda)\sum_{n=1}^{H-t-1}\lambda^{n-1}G_t^{(n)}+\lambda^{H-t-1}G_t^{(H-t)}\\&=r_t+\gamma[(1-\lambda)V(s_{t+1})+\lambda G_{t+1}^\lambda],\\G_H^\lambda&=V(s_H).\end{aligned}Gt(n)​Gtλ​GHλ​​=j=0∑n−1​γjrt+j​+γnV(st+n​),=(1−λ)n=1∑H−t−1​λn−1Gt(n)​+λH−t−1Gt(H−t)​=rt​+γ[(1−λ)V(st+1​)+λGt+1λ​],=V(sH​).​

To obtain the recursion, take rₜ out of every n-step term, whose weights sum to one. The n=1 bootstrap contributes γ(1−λ)V(sₜ₊₁); factor γλ from all remaining terms and recognize the same mixture starting at t+1. At λ=0 only a one-step target remains. At λ=1 the target becomes the full truncated return plus its final bootstrap. These endpoints trade reliance on intermediate values against exposure to longer model rollouts; they do not eliminate approximation error.

Now write continuous imagined dynamics as sₜ₊₁=Fφ(sₜ,πθ(sₜ,ξₜ),εₜ), with sampled noise ξ,ε held fixed during pathwise differentiation. If Dₜ=∂sₜ/∂θ, the chain rule gives:

Dt+1=FsDt+Fa(πsDt+πθ)=(Fs+Faπs)Dt+Faπθ,∂r(st,at)∂θ=rsDt+ra(πsDt+πθ).\begin{aligned}D_{t+1}&=F_sD_t+F_a(\pi_sD_t+\pi_\theta)\\&=(F_s+F_a\pi_s)D_t+F_a\pi_\theta,\\\frac{\partial r(s_t,a_t)}{\partial\theta}&=r_sD_t+r_a(\pi_sD_t+\pi_\theta).\end{aligned}Dt+1​∂θ∂r(st​,at​)​​=Fs​Dt​+Fa​(πs​Dt​+πθ​)=(Fs​+Fa​πs​)Dt​+Fa​πθ​,=rs​Dt​+ra​(πs​Dt​+πθ​).​

Freezing φ prevents updates to model parameters, but the Jacobians F_s and F_a remain in the actor gradient. Removing them would remove the pathwise credit signal. For discrete actions or latents, a score-function estimator or a biased straight-through surrogate is needed. The derivative optimizes the learned simulator; a precise gradient through an inaccurate transition can still push the real policy in the wrong direction.

Exercise — Verify the recursion against the mixture

Let H=3, γ=0.9, λ=0.8, rewards (1,2,3), and bootstrap values V(s₁)=4, V(s₂)=5, V(s₃)=6. Compute G₀^λ using both formulas.

Show worked solution

Start at the horizon and work backward:

G3=6,G2=3+0.9×6=8.4,G1=2+0.9(0.2×5+0.8×8.4)=8.948,G0=1+0.9(0.2×4+0.8×8.948)=8.16256.\begin{aligned}G_3&=6,\\G_2&=3+0.9\times6=8.4,\\G_1&=2+0.9(0.2\times5+0.8\times8.4)=8.948,\\G_0&=1+0.9(0.2\times4+0.8\times8.948)=8.16256.\end{aligned}G3​G2​G1​G0​​=6,=3+0.9×6=8.4,=2+0.9(0.2×5+0.8×8.4)=8.948,=1+0.9(0.2×4+0.8×8.948)=8.16256.​

The n-step targets are G₀⁽¹⁾=4.6, G₀⁽²⁾=6.85, and G₀⁽³⁾=9.604. Their weights are 0.2, 0.16, and 0.64, so 0.2×4.6+0.16×6.85+0.64×9.604=8.16256. Agreement checks the transition indexing and the final truncated weight, two common implementation mistakes.

5.2 DreamerV2: discrete stochastic states and KL balancing

DreamerV2 replaces Gaussian stochastic latents with a vector of categorical variables, in the reported architecture 32 categoricals with 32 classes each. The combinatorial state space is large, while each individual factor is easy to parameterize and sample. Discrete latents can represent multimodal structure without forcing it into a unimodal Gaussian. They do not by themselves identify meaningful objects or guarantee epistemic calibration. [6]

Original Figure 2 shows posterior z and prior z-hat at every step. Both are distributions over categorical factors; the right-hand grid illustrates their factorization. The green KL arrows train the transition distribution toward states obtained from observations. The purple recurrent chain retains temporal information. Notice that the image decoder is attached to the posterior state during model learning, whereas imagined actor training uses the prior state.

Sampling a one-hot categorical has no ordinary derivative. DreamerV2 uses a straight-through estimator: take a discrete sample in the forward pass, but substitute the derivative of its probabilities in the backward pass. This is a biased gradient estimator, not exact differentiation through a discrete draw. Its practical role is to make the stochastic representation trainable with ordinary automatic differentiation.

zsample=one_hot⁡(Categorical⁡(probs)),zST=stop_gradient⁡(zsample−probs)+probs,LKL=αDKL(stop_gradient⁡(q)∥p)+(1−α)DKL(q∥stop_gradient⁡(p)).\begin{aligned}z_{\mathrm{sample}}&=\operatorname{one\_hot}(\operatorname{Categorical}(\mathrm{probs})),\\z_{\mathrm{ST}}&=\operatorname{stop\_gradient}(z_{\mathrm{sample}}-\mathrm{probs})+\mathrm{probs},\\\mathcal L_{\mathrm{KL}}&=\alpha D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\operatorname{stop\_gradient}(q)\|p)\\&\quad+(1-\alpha)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|\operatorname{stop\_gradient}(p)).\end{aligned}zsample​zST​LKL​​=one_hot(Categorical(probs)),=stop_gradient(zsample​−probs)+probs,=αDKL​(stop_gradient(q)∥p)+(1−α)DKL​(q∥stop_gradient(p)).​

The second equation is KL balancing. The same KL has two jobs: teach the prior to predict the posterior, and regularize the posterior toward the prior. Early in learning the prior is poor, so imposing equal pressure in both directions can destroy useful representations. Balancing gives the prior a stronger learning signal without simply multiplying both gradients by one β. In DreamerV2 the commonly reported balance is α=0.8. Actor learning also distinguishes score-function gradients from dynamics gradients; different action spaces need not benefit from the same mixture.

5.3 DreamerV3: stable units, target distributions, and gradient scales

DreamerV3's contribution is a coordinated training recipe that works over many domains with one set of hyperparameters. It is tempting to summarize this as a bigger Dreamer, but the more useful interpretation is control of interacting gradient scales. Observation magnitudes, rewards, return outliers, latent KL, and policy entropy can differ enormously between a walking robot and Minecraft. [7]

The signed logarithm handles positive and negative quantities while compressing large magnitudes:

symlog⁡(x)=sign⁡(x)log⁡(1+∣x∣),symexp⁡(y)=sign⁡(y)(e∣y∣−1),Ldyn=max⁡(1  nat,DKL(stop_gradient⁡(q)∥p)),Lrep=max⁡(1  nat,DKL(q∥stop_gradient⁡(p))).\begin{aligned}\operatorname{symlog}(x)&=\operatorname{sign}(x)\log(1+|x|),\\\operatorname{symexp}(y)&=\operatorname{sign}(y)(e^{|y|}-1),\\\mathcal L_{\mathrm{dyn}}&=\max(1\;\mathrm{nat},D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\operatorname{stop\_gradient}(q)\|p)),\\\mathcal L_{\mathrm{rep}}&=\max(1\;\mathrm{nat},D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|\operatorname{stop\_gradient}(p))).\end{aligned}symlog(x)symexp(y)Ldyn​Lrep​​=sign(x)log(1+∣x∣),=sign(y)(e∣y∣−1),=max(1nat,DKL​(stop_gradient(q)∥p)),=max(1nat,DKL​(q∥stop_gradient(p))).​

“Free bits” clip the KL penalty from below: when the divergence is already below the threshold, that regularizer contributes no gradient. It does not cap excessive KL. Together with a weaker representation loss, this lets the state retain useful information without being driven to a trivial predictable encoding. A small uniform mixture in categorical probabilities prevents distributions from becoming exactly deterministic and avoids extreme KL behavior.

For stochastic rewards and values, two-hot regression encodes a scalar target as weights on neighboring bins and minimizes categorical cross-entropy. With transformed or exponentially spaced support, this handles broad numeric ranges while avoiding a squared-error gradient whose scale grows directly with the target. Decode by the appropriate expected value over support, not by casually applying symexp⁡\operatorname{symexp}symexp to any averaged transformed number; nonlinear transforms and expectations do not commute.

The actor uses a score-function objective with an advantage scaled by a smoothed return range. The range is based on robust percentiles and is floored, so tiny sparse-reward variation is not amplified into large policy noise. This is different from forcing every batch of advantages to unit variance. The entropy term should remain meaningful when attainable reward is scarce. Later versions of the paper also detail value learning on replay trajectories and stabilization of bootstrapped targets; experimental claims should track the specific released recipe.

Original Figure 6 is an argument for a system of techniques, not one magic layer. The left panels vary robustness components and learning signals; the vertical axis is task performance, not reconstruction loss. The right panels change model size and replay ratio, with horizontal axes in environment steps. More replay reuses the same real interactions but consumes more accelerator work. The plots therefore establish improved sample use and stable scaling under that setup, not free improvements at fixed wall-clock cost. Removing reconstruction gradients and removing reward/value gradients affect representation learning differently, illustrating the tension between general information and task relevance.

Derivation: two-hot targets preserve a scalar moment, not every nonlinear transform

Let ordered scalar support values be b₁<…<bK. For y between adjacent support points bⱼ and bⱼ₊₁, define a categorical target t with only two nonzero entries. Solve the two equations tⱼ+tⱼ₊₁=1 and tⱼbⱼ+tⱼ₊₁bⱼ₊₁=y:

tj=bj+1−ybj+1−bj,tj+1=y−bjbj+1−bj,∑itibi=y,L=−∑itilog⁡pi,p=softmax⁡(logits),∂L∂logiti=pi−ti.\begin{aligned}t_j&=\frac{b_{j+1}-y}{b_{j+1}-b_j},\quad t_{j+1}=\frac{y-b_j}{b_{j+1}-b_j},\\\sum_it_ib_i&=y,\\\mathcal L&=-\sum_it_i\log p_i,\quad p=\operatorname{softmax}(\mathrm{logits}),\\\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\mathrm{logit}_i}&=p_i-t_i.\end{aligned}tj​i∑​ti​bi​L∂logiti​∂L​​=bj+1​−bj​bj+1​−y​,tj+1​=bj+1​−bj​y−bj​​,=y,=−i∑​ti​logpi​,p=softmax(logits),=pi​−ti​.​

The last result follows by differentiating log softmax and using Σt=1. Each logit derivative is between −1 and 1 regardless of y's magnitude; a raw squared-error derivative instead scales with prediction error. This helps explain the numerical attraction of distributional scalar regression, although gradients through earlier network layers can still be large. When the predictor matches the conditional mean target distribution, taking its expectation over these same support values recovers E[y|context] for in-range targets.

There are two different designs: interpolate directly between exponentially spaced scalar values, or transform y first and interpolate in the transformed space. They produce different targets and decoders. For a nonlinear g, g⁻¹(E[g(Y)]) generally differs from E[Y]. With probability one-half on transformed values 0 and 2, averaging in that space then applying symexp yields e−1≈1.718, whereas averaging the corresponding original values yields (e²−1)/2≈3.195. One must follow the paper version and implementation's support definition.

Targets outside the support require clipping or another explicit rule; clipping destroys exact moment preservation for those targets. Two-hot regression controls an optimization representation. It does not make the predicted reward distribution calibrated or remove uncertainty in long-horizon returns.

Exercise — Construct a target and its gradient

For support (−1,0,2), target y=0.5, and prediction p=(0.1,0.7,0.2), compute the two-hot target, decoded prediction, and gradient with respect to the three logits.

Show worked solution

The target lies between 0 and 2, so t=(0,0.75,0.25). Its support mean is 0.75×0+0.25×2=0.5. The model's decoded mean is 0.1×(−1)+0.7×0+0.2×2=0.3. Differentiating cross-entropy gives p−t=(0.1,−0.05,−0.05). Gradient descent lowers the −1 logit and raises the other two relative to it. A single step is not guaranteed to produce the exact target distribution because softmax couples all coordinates.

5.4 Variants reveal what the base loop leaves unresolved

Plan2Explore uses disagreement among latent predictions as an intrinsic reward to learn an exploration policy before a downstream task is supplied. It turns epistemic novelty into a control objective. Surprise due solely to irreducible noise is less useful than learnable disagreement; the design of the prediction ensemble matters. DayDreamer applies imagination learning to real robots, where continuous collection, resets, action timing, and safe operating envelopes matter as much as benchmark sample counts. [24] [25]

Action-free pretraining from videos (APV) separates broad visual dynamics pretraining from later action-conditioned learning through a stacked latent model. It anticipates the video-to-action gap encountered by larger systems. HarmonyDream studies imbalance between observation and reward modeling and adjusts their loss weights. STORM (2023) replaces the recurrent sequence component with a stochastic Transformer while retaining latent imagination. These variants alter data use, objective weighting, or memory structure; none eliminates model exploitation merely by improving the sequence backbone. [23] [26] [27]

6 · Era II-B: MuZero and EfficientZero model what search needs

6.1 Value relevance rather than pixel reconstruction

MuZero starts from a different premise: to select an action, a model need not regenerate the entire observation. It needs to provide reliable rewards, values, and policy priors along the action sequences considered by search. Three learned functions implement this premise: representation h maps a history to hidden state; dynamics g maps hidden state and action to the next hidden state and reward; prediction f produces a policy prior and value. [9]

s0=h(observation history),(r^k,sk)=g(sk−1,ak),(p^k,v^k)=f(sk),L=∑k[ℓreward(r^k,rk)+ℓvalue(v^k,target returnk)+ℓpolicy(p^k,search policyk)]+regularization.\begin{aligned}s_0&=h(\text{observation history}),\\(\hat r_k,s_k)&=g(s_{k-1},a_k),\quad(\hat p_k,\hat v_k)=f(s_k),\\\mathcal L&=\sum_k\big[\ell_{\mathrm{reward}}(\hat r_k,r_k)+\ell_{\mathrm{value}}(\hat v_k,\mathrm{target\ return}_k)\\&\qquad+\ell_{\mathrm{policy}}(\hat p_k,\mathrm{search\ policy}_k)\big]+\mathrm{regularization}.\end{aligned}s0​(r^k​,sk​)L​=h(observation history),=g(sk−1​,ak​),(p^​k​,v^k​)=f(sk​),=k∑​[ℓreward​(r^k​,rk​)+ℓvalue​(v^k​,target returnk​)+ℓpolicy​(p^​k​,search policyk​)]+regularization.​

Original Figure 1 has three distinct graphs. Search expands hidden states and backs up predicted values. Acting applies the chosen action to the real game. Training unrolls recorded action sequences through the learned dynamics and supervises rewards, returns, and search-improved policies. No image decoder is required. The hidden-state circles should therefore not be read as miniature physical simulators whose coordinates correspond to board pieces or pixels. Their meaning is defined by how well they support these predictive targets.

MCTS combines an estimated action value with an exploration bonus involving the policy prior and visit counts. Repeated simulations focus computation on promising actions while preserving some exploration. Backup aggregates predicted rewards and leaf values along the path. The visit distribution at the root then supplies a stronger policy target than the raw network prior. Model learning, search, and policy improvement form a coupled loop: changes in the model change search targets, which change data collection and future training targets.

A useful abstraction is value equivalence: two models can differ in predicted observations yet agree on the Bellman updates needed by a set of policies and value functions. This gives a principled reason to omit irrelevant details. It does not mean a reward/value-trained model is sufficient for every future reward function. Change the task so that a formerly irrelevant object matters and the representation may have erased exactly the information now required. [22]

6.2 EfficientZero: three responses to the small-data regime

MuZero's original successes include substantial search and interaction budgets. EfficientZero addresses Atari 100k with additions targeted at that data-limited regime. First, a self-supervised consistency objective aligns a latent predicted by dynamics with an encoding of the actual next observation. This supplies dense representation supervision even when reward is sparse. A stop-gradient target and appropriate predictor avoid asking the entire system to minimize the distance by collapsing to a constant. [10]

Second, a value-prefix predictor models cumulative reward along a short unroll. Simply summing independent one-step reward errors can accumulate bias; sequence-level reward prediction gives the model temporal context for that prefix. It does not remove the need for a terminal value estimate. Third, model-based off-policy correction improves value targets for replay data collected by older policies. A target based on a stale behavior trajectory can bias evaluation of the current improved policy. EfficientZero adjusts the effective bootstrap and reanalysis to use current model/search information.

The lessons generalize beyond Atari. Representation consistency addresses sparse learning signals, reward-prefix prediction addresses accumulation of reward error, and replay correction addresses policy nonstationarity. These are separable mechanisms and should be tested separately. A stronger search-based score may still require more online computation than an actor-only method. Comparing score at equal environment steps without reporting simulations, training updates, and action latency leaves the main resource tradeoff unresolved.

Derivation: value equivalence is relative to a test-function class

For a policy π and test value function v, a model's Bellman operator is Tπv(s)=rπ(s)+γΣₛ′Pπ(s′|s)v(s′). Consider an approximate model with hats. It is value-equivalent for policy class Π and function class V when the two operators agree for every π∈Π and v∈V. This is a precise, restricted condition, unlike the statement that its latent states “look useful.”

(Tπ−T^π)v=(rπ−r^π)+γ(Pπ−P^π)v,V=span⁡{v1,…,vm}.Basis agreement extends to linear combinationswhen the reward term is matched separately.\begin{aligned}(T^\pi-\hat T^\pi)v&=(r^\pi-\hat r^\pi)+\gamma(P^\pi-\hat P^\pi)v,\\\mathcal V&=\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}.\\&\text{Basis agreement extends to linear combinations}\\&\text{when the reward term is matched separately.}\end{aligned}(Tπ−T^π)vV​=(rπ−r^π)+γ(Pπ−P^π)v,=span{v1​,…,vm​}.Basis agreement extends to linear combinationswhen the reward term is matched separately.​

The condition constrains expected projections of the next-state distribution rather than necessarily the full distribution. If V contains indicators of every state and rewards match, those projections identify every transition probability. If V is small, many physically different models are equivalent for the tested questions. This explains both the efficiency and the transfer limitation of task-oriented representations.

Fixed-point consequence. Suppose vπ is the true value of a policy, vπ∈V, and equivalence holds at that function. Then vπ=Tπvπ=T̂πvπ. Because a discounted Markov model's Bellman operator is a γ-contraction in sup norm, it has a unique fixed point, so vπ=v̂π. The conclusion requires the relevant true value function to lie in the tested class; fitting finitely many bootstrapped targets does not establish that premise.

MuZero's reward, value, and search-policy targets encourage decision-relevant predictions, but its practical neural training objective is not a universal proof of value equivalence for all policies or new rewards. EfficientZero's additional consistency targets broaden the representation pressure without changing this logical limitation.

Exercise — A model that passes one value test and fails another

At state s, the real transition goes to u and the model transition goes to v, with zero immediate reward and γ=0.9. A test function assigns both u and v the value 2. Does the Bellman test detect the error? Repeat with w(u)=1 and w(v)=0. What does this show about transfer?

Show worked solution

For the first function, both backups equal 0+0.9×2=1.8, so this test cannot distinguish the transitions. For w, the real backup is 0.9 and the model backup is 0. The error becomes visible as soon as the function class contains a distinction relevant to the new task. Passing a finite set of value tests is therefore weaker than recovering the environment dynamics; transfer needs the new reward/value directions to be represented or newly learned.

6.3 Why task-oriented models can both help and hurt generalization

Removing reconstruction can eliminate nuisance competition and make planning cheaper. But it also removes a broad diagnostic signal. If all training rewards ignore color, a color change may be invisible in the latent, even though a new instruction requires selecting the red object. An observation-generating model is not guaranteed to solve transfer either; it may model color accurately while failing to bind it to a controllable object.

The useful question is therefore: which distinctions must survive for the family of decisions we intend to support? Test changed rewards, changed action distributions, and rare events rather than treating “general-purpose” as an architectural property. Search can sometimes compensate for a weak policy; it cannot recover a state distinction that the model has already discarded.

7 · TD-MPC and TD-MPC2: continuous control with a short trusted model and a long value tail

TD-MPC joins task-oriented latent dynamics, temporal-difference learning, and model predictive control. Continuous actions make exhaustive tree expansion expensive; instead the planner samples trajectories, rolls them through a learned latent model, sums predicted rewards, and appends a terminal value. A learned policy prior supplies plausible trajectories to the sampler. This combines an actor's reusable behavior with local online improvement. [13]

z0=encoder⁡(ot),zh+1=dynamics⁡(zh,ah),J(A)=∑h=0H−1γhr^(zh,ah)+γHQ^(zH,aH),wi∝exp⁡ ⁣(Ji−max⁡jJjtemperature).Update action-sequence mean/variance;execute a0, infer fresh state, and replan.\begin{aligned}z_0&=\operatorname{encoder}(o_t),\quad z_{h+1}=\operatorname{dynamics}(z_h,a_h),\\J(A)&=\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}\gamma^h\hat r(z_h,a_h)+\gamma^H\hat Q(z_H,a_H),\\w_i&\propto\exp\!\left(\frac{J_i-\max_jJ_j}{\mathrm{temperature}}\right).\\&\text{Update action-sequence mean/variance;}\\&\text{execute }a_0\text{, infer fresh state, and replan.}\end{aligned}z0​J(A)wi​​=encoder(ot​),zh+1​=dynamics(zh​,ah​),=h=0∑H−1​γhr^(zh​,ah​)+γHQ^​(zH​,aH​),∝exp(temperatureJi​−maxj​Jj​​).Update action-sequence mean/variance;execute a0​, infer fresh state, and replan.​

The short horizon limits model error, while the terminal critic represents consequences beyond that horizon. The actor prior improves search efficiency but can restrict coverage if all candidates resemble a poor behavior. Gaussian exploration around the plan introduces alternatives. Warm-starting and action bounds are implementation details with algorithmic effects: a clipped sampling distribution differs from an unconstrained Gaussian, and a stale warm start can resist abrupt task changes.

Derivation: terminal values shorten planning only when their error is controlled

Fix a candidate action sequence of length H, initial state s₀, discount γ, and exact dynamics for the moment. Let its objective use H rewards followed by a terminal value V. Replace V by V̂ with uniform error at most δ. Only the final term changes:

J(A)=∑t=0H−1γtr(st,at)+γHV(sH),∣J^(A)−J(A)∣≤γHδ.\begin{aligned}J(A)&=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^tr(s_t,a_t)+\gamma^HV(s_H),\\|\hat J(A)-J(A)|&\le\gamma^H\delta.\end{aligned}J(A)∣J^(A)−J(A)∣​=t=0∑H−1​γtr(st​,at​)+γHV(sH​),≤γHδ.​

Let A* maximize J and Â maximize Ĵ over the same candidate set. Add and subtract the approximate scores:

J(A∗)−J(A^)=[J(A∗)−J^(A∗)]+[J^(A∗)−J^(A^)]+[J^(A^)−J(A^)]≤γHδ+0+γHδ=2γHδ.\begin{aligned}J(A^*)-J(\hat A)&=[J(A^*)-\hat J(A^*)]\\&\quad+[\hat J(A^*)-\hat J(\hat A)]\\&\quad+[\hat J(\hat A)-J(\hat A)]\\&\le\gamma^H\delta+0+\gamma^H\delta=2\gamma^H\delta.\end{aligned}J(A∗)−J(A^)​=[J(A∗)−J^(A∗)]+[J^(A∗)−J^(A^)]+[J^(A^)−J(A^)]≤γHδ+0+γHδ=2γHδ.​

The middle term is nonpositive because Â is an exact maximizer of the approximate score. An optimizer with error η adds η to the bound. Longer H suppresses terminal-value error, but a learned transition introduces a competing term. For deterministic dynamics, assume a common initial state, uniform one-step transition error at most ε, and an L-Lipschitz transition in state for each fixed action. Repeatedly applying eₜ₊₁≤Leₜ+ε gives eₜ≤εΣⱼ₌₀ᵗ⁻¹Lʲ. If reward error at identical states is at most εr, rewards are Lr-Lipschitz, and the true terminal value is LV-Lipschitz, then:

∣J^(A)−J(A)∣≤∑t=0H−1γt(εr+Lret)+γH(δ+LVeH).|\hat J(A)-J(A)|\le\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^t(\varepsilon_r+L_re_t)+\gamma^H(\delta+L_Ve_H).∣J^(A)−J(A)∣≤t=0∑H−1​γt(εr​+Lr​et​)+γH(δ+LV​eH​).

Each reward difference was split into model error at the same state and sensitivity to using the wrong state. The terminal term is split similarly. This is the mathematical reason short model rollouts plus a value tail can help: increasing H decreases one error source and can increase another. All bounds must hold uniformly over the candidates the optimizer might select. Validation error averaged under the data distribution does not provide that guarantee.

Exercise — When is a predicted plan ordering certified?

With exact dynamics, γ=0.9, H=4, and terminal error δ=0.5, calculate the score-error bound. Two plans have predicted returns differing by 0.8. Is the predicted ordering guaranteed under these assumptions? What if the difference is 0.4?

Show worked solution
γHδ=0.94×0.5=0.32805,Worst score-difference error=2×0.32805=0.65610.\begin{aligned}\gamma^H\delta&=0.9^4\times0.5=0.32805,\\\text{Worst score-difference error}&=2\times0.32805=0.65610.\end{aligned}γHδWorst score-difference error​=0.94×0.5=0.32805,=2×0.32805=0.65610.​

A predicted gap of 0.8 remains positive even if the preferred plan is overestimated and its competitor underestimated by the maximum amount; the minimum true gap is 0.1439. A gap of 0.4 can change sign, so the ordering is uncertified. This is not a claim that it will be wrong. Learned transition error, optimizer error, or a nonuniform terminal bound would require additional terms.

7.1 TD-MPC2's stability recipe

TD-MPC2 replaces fragile scale-dependent choices with a coordinated architecture and objective. It learns a decoder-free latent transition, reward predictor, ensemble of Q-functions, and stochastic maximum-entropy policy prior. Reward and value prediction use discrete regression in a transformed space. An ensemble reduces optimistic value errors; the reported setup uses five critics and a target derived from two sampled members. [14]

SimNorm partitions a latent vector into small groups and applies a softmax within each group. Each group lies on a simplex, with nonnegative entries summing to one. This controls activation growth and encourages a structured sparse representation without sampling a discrete latent. It is not the same mechanism as DreamerV2's categorical variable, even if their grids look similar.

SimNorm⁡(zg)i=ezi/τ∑j∈gezj/τ,∣g∣=V,Lmodel⊃∥dynamics⁡(zt,at)−stop_gradient⁡(encoder⁡(ot+1))∥2+Lreward classification+Lvalue classification (bootstrapped).\begin{aligned}\operatorname{SimNorm}(z_g)_i&=\frac{e^{z_i/\tau}}{\sum_{j\in g}e^{z_j/\tau}},\quad|g|=V,\\\mathcal L_{\mathrm{model}}&\supset\|\operatorname{dynamics}(z_t,a_t)-\operatorname{stop\_gradient}(\operatorname{encoder}(o_{t+1}))\|^2\\&\quad+\mathcal L_{\mathrm{reward\ classification}}\\&\quad+\mathcal L_{\mathrm{value\ classification\ (bootstrapped)}}.\end{aligned}SimNorm(zg​)i​Lmodel​​=∑j∈g​ezj​/τezi​/τ​,∣g∣=V,⊃∥dynamics(zt​,at​)−stop_gradient(encoder(ot+1​))∥2+Lreward classification​+Lvalue classification (bootstrapped)​.​

The latent consistency loss connects imagined states to states inferred from actual observations. Reward and value gradients make the representation useful for control. Task embeddings enable multi-task training, while masks handle differences in action dimensions. A single model across embodiments must know which action coordinates are valid; padding unused dimensions alone is not a complete semantic definition of the action space.

Original Figure 7 compares model size on multi-task datasets. The horizontal axis is parameter count; the vertical axis is a normalized score across the specified tasks. TD-MPC2 improves as model capacity grows, whereas naively enlarging the earlier TD-MPC baseline degrades in the shown settings. This is evidence that stabilization determines whether added capacity can be used. The right visualization of task embeddings suggests learned structure, but a two-dimensional embedding plot is not proof of causal task similarity or transfer guarantees.

The paper reports 104 tasks for its broad single-task study and an 80-task setting for a large multi-task agent. These are different experiments. A 317M model trained on an 80-task dataset is not an agent that learned all 104 tasks under the same data and computation budget. For practical comparison with Dreamer, check the observation modality, online versus offline learning, planning iterations, and action-time latency before interpreting a normalized score.

8 · Era III: detailed generative simulators — IRIS, STORM, and DIAMOND

8.1 IRIS: an environment becomes a language of visual tokens

IRIS encodes each frame into a small grid of discrete codes and learns an autoregressive Transformer over interleaved frame codes and actions. The tokenizer maps image patches or local feature vectors to codebook entries; the dynamics model predicts the next visual token conditioned on preceding frame/action tokens and the earlier tokens of the current frame. Reward and termination prediction complete the simulator used for actor–critic learning. [15]

zt=E(ot)∈{1,…,V}K,p(zt+1∣history,at)=∏j=1Kp(zt+1j∣history,at,zt+1<j).Training:reconstruction + codebook/commitment objectives;transition-token CE + reward/termination objectives.Imagination:sample tokens→decode→actor action→repeat.\begin{aligned}z_t&=E(o_t)\in\{1,\ldots,V\}^K,\\p(z_{t+1}\mid\mathrm{history},a_t)&=\prod_{j=1}^Kp(z_{t+1}^j\mid\mathrm{history},a_t,z_{t+1}^{<j}).\\\text{Training:}&\quad\text{reconstruction + codebook/commitment objectives;}\\&\quad\text{transition-token CE + reward/termination objectives}.\\\text{Imagination:}&\quad\text{sample tokens}\to\text{decode}\to\text{actor action}\to\text{repeat}.\end{aligned}zt​p(zt+1​∣history,at​)Training:Imagination:​=E(ot​)∈{1,…,V}K,=j=1∏K​p(zt+1j​∣history,at​,zt+1<j​).reconstruction + codebook/commitment objectives;transition-token CE + reward/termination objectives.sample tokens→decode→actor action→repeat.​

Original Figure 1 exposes the cost that the word “Transformer” hides. Green arrows connect the encoder/decoder and frame representation; blue arrows carry the generative dynamics through the token sequence; the policy consumes the imagined observations. Time advances only after a frame's visual codes have been generated. With K tokens per frame, one environment step can require many sequential token predictions. Reducing K accelerates imagination but tightens the representational bottleneck. Unlike the Dreamer latent actor, IRIS uses decoded images in its imagined interaction loop.

The tokenizer's objective is largely perceptual and reconstructive. A tiny projectile, timer digit, or one-pixel collision cue may contribute little to average image error but determine the optimal action. Once the tokenizer discards that cue, a perfect token dynamics model cannot reconstruct it. This creates a two-stage error decomposition: representation loss before dynamics learning, followed by prediction error within the retained representation. Increasing Transformer size addresses only the second.

IRIS demonstrates that generated observations can sustain policy improvement with limited real Atari interaction. Its same-prefix multiple-future visualizations also show why matching one recorded future pixel for pixel is not always appropriate: unseen opponents may legitimately appear in different ways. The relevant question is whether the conditional distribution preserves the mechanics and reward consequences, not whether a stochastic rollout reproduces an arbitrary random seed.

STORM retains stochastic latent modeling while using a Transformer for sequence memory. It belongs near IRIS historically, but it does not simply replace every RSSM state by a sequence of image tokens. The contrast is useful: Transformer sequence modeling, stochastic state design, visual tokenization, and actor observation choice are independent axes. A paper may improve one axis while retaining the other three. [27]

8.2 DIAMOND: diffusion removes the hard token bottleneck, but adds a sampling budget

DIAMOND predicts visual observations with a conditional diffusion model, conditioning on recent observations and actions. It trains a denoiser on a corrupted next frame, then generates the next observation through several denoising evaluations. An actor–critic learns in these generated observations. Reward and episode termination remain explicit learned quantities; attractive video is insufficient if reward or termination is wrong. [16]

xnoisy=xnext+σε,ε∼N(0,I),Dθ(xnoisy,σ,history,actions)≈xnext,L=E[w(σ)∥Dθ(xnoisy,σ,context)−xnext∥2].Inference:noise→denoising updatesnext frame.World time t and noise time σ are distinct axes.\begin{aligned}x_{\mathrm{noisy}}&=x_{\mathrm{next}}+\sigma\varepsilon,\quad\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I),\\D_\theta(x_{\mathrm{noisy}},\sigma,\mathrm{history},\mathrm{actions})&\approx x_{\mathrm{next}},\\\mathcal L&=\mathbb E[w(\sigma)\|D_\theta(x_{\mathrm{noisy}},\sigma,\mathrm{context})-x_{\mathrm{next}}\|^2].\\\text{Inference:}&\quad\text{noise}\xrightarrow{\text{denoising updates}}\text{next frame}.\\&\text{World time }t\text{ and noise time }\sigma\text{ are distinct axes.}\end{aligned}xnoisy​Dθ​(xnoisy​,σ,history,actions)LInference:​=xnext​+σε,ε∼N(0,I),≈xnext​,=E[w(σ)∥Dθ​(xnoisy​,σ,context)−xnext​∥2].noisedenoising updates​next frame.World time t and noise time σ are distinct axes.​

The paper uses the EDM parameterization and preconditioning rather than directly adopting a standard DDPM setup. The denoiser combines a skip connection from the noisy input with a scaled network prediction, controlling the range presented to the neural network at different noise levels. This is more than a cosmetic choice when generated frames become the next step's conditioning context: small systematic errors can be repeatedly amplified.

Original Figure 3 compares long free-running rollouts under DDPM and EDM formulations. Columns move forward in environment time, while rows change the number of denoising steps. The DDPM examples visibly drift at small sampling budgets; EDM is more stable in the shown setting. This figure is evidence about autoregressive deployment robustness under few function evaluations. It is not evidence that all diffusion models are physically accurate, nor that one denoising step is generally sufficient.

A one-step denoiser tends toward a conditional mean when the future is ambiguous. If an opponent can move left or right, averaging those futures can erase or smear it. More denoising steps can express distinct modes. DIAMOND uses three steps in its reported Atari experiments as a quality/cost compromise. The important unit of cost is the number of model evaluations per environment transition, multiplied by the number of imagined transitions needed for policy training.

Original Figure 5 compares generated sequences from IRIS and DIAMOND. The white boxes draw attention to small objects and local consistency across frames. These regions may occupy very few pixels but strongly affect control. This supports the paper's claim that visual detail can be decision-relevant. It does not show that all pixels deserve equal weight, or that the entire performance gap is caused solely by tokenizer quality: the complete agents differ in architecture, optimization, and rollout cost.

DIAMOND's appendix makes the computational tradeoff unusually concrete: it reports approximately 2.9 training days for the studied configuration, compared with 4.1 for IRIS and under one day for the compared DreamerV3 configuration, alongside parameter counts and Atari scores. Those are reported implementation measurements, not hardware-normalized scaling laws. They are nevertheless more informative than comparing only environment samples. A “sample-efficient” model can be expensive to imagine with.

Derivation: noise prediction learns a score field, not a single average future

Let X be a clean future frame conditional on history c, and form Y=αX+σε with independent ε∼N(0,I). Hold noise level α,σ>0 fixed during the derivation. A denoiser minimizing E∥ε−f(Y,c)∥² satisfies f*(y,c)=E[ε|Y=y,c]. This follows by writing ε−f=(ε−E[ε|Y,c])+(E[ε|Y,c]−f); the conditional cross term is zero, so the minimum occurs at the conditional mean.

pσ(y∣c)=∫p(x∣c)N(y;αx,σ2I) dx,∇ylog⁡pσ(y∣c)=∫p(x∣c)N(y;αx,σ2I)(−y−αxσ2) dxpσ(y∣c)=−E[ε∣y,c]σ=−f∗(y,c)σ.\begin{aligned}p_\sigma(y\mid c)&=\int p(x\mid c)\mathcal N(y;\alpha x,\sigma^2I)\,dx,\\\nabla_y\log p_\sigma(y\mid c)&=\frac{\int p(x\mid c)\mathcal N(y;\alpha x,\sigma^2I)\left(-\frac{y-\alpha x}{\sigma^2}\right)\,dx}{p_\sigma(y\mid c)}\\&=-\frac{\mathbb E[\varepsilon\mid y,c]}\sigma=-\frac{f^*(y,c)}\sigma.\end{aligned}pσ​(y∣c)∇y​logpσ​(y∣c)​=∫p(x∣c)N(y;αx,σ2I)dx,=pσ​(y∣c)∫p(x∣c)N(y;αx,σ2I)(−σ2y−αx​)dx​=−σE[ε∣y,c]​=−σf∗(y,c)​.​

The second line differentiates the Gaussian likelihood under the integral, assuming the usual integrability conditions. Thus an MSE-trained noise predictor identifies the score of the noisy conditional distribution. A reverse diffusion procedure uses score estimates at many noise levels to transport samples toward the data distribution. This explains how a family of conditional-mean predictors can generate multiple futures rather than outputting one unconditional mean image.

Numerical sanity check. If X∈{−1,+1} with equal probability, α=1, and Y=0, symmetry gives E[X|Y]=0 even though zero is not a valid clean mode. A one-step posterior-mean reconstruction returns that midpoint. A properly sampled reverse process can end near either −1 or +1. Fewer solver steps, model error, and deterministic approximations alter this behavior; the score identity alone is not a theorem about a particular three-step implementation.

This is why DIAMOND's sampling budget belongs in a control comparison. Its denoiser objective can be correct while the resulting finite-step simulator still blurs small task-relevant details or accumulates rollout drift. Test the entire sampled transition kernel under action interventions, rather than only its denoising loss.

9 · Passive video, latent actions, and predictive embeddings

9.1 Genie: discover an action interface without button labels

Genie learns three components from videos: a video tokenizer, a latent-action model, and an action-conditioned dynamics model. The latent-action encoder observes a transition and compresses what changed into a small discrete code. A decoder trained to predict the next frame from the previous context and that code gives the action representation a learning signal. During interactive generation, a user selects latent codes instead of inferring them from a known future. [17]

Original Figure 3 shows two parallel compressions of a video. The video tokenizer produces state-like visual tokens; the latent-action model produces transition codes. The dynamics model receives both. The latent-action encoder is allowed to observe information that an acting policy would not yet know, because its job during training is to infer an explanation of a recorded change. At inference the user supplies a code and the dynamics model predicts the consequence. Confusing these two stages would amount to giving the controller future observations.

This is an identifiability problem. A discovered code need not mean “move left” in a universal physical coordinate frame; its semantics emerge from the dataset and model. The mapping can be permuted without changing likelihood. Worse, a transition code may encode camera movement, an external object, or an unobserved actor rather than the controllable agent. A small bottleneck encourages compact factors of change, but does not mathematically guarantee causal disentanglement.

Genie's spatial–temporal Transformer factorizes attention within frames and across time. The dynamics model uses masked-token prediction and iterative generation within a frame rather than exactly IRIS's left-to-right token mechanism. The reported platformer dataset contains roughly 30,000 hours after filtering, and the main scaled model has 11B parameters. These choices move the setting far beyond Atari 100k; the interaction data budget and pretraining distribution are part of the result, not implementation footnotes.

Genie 2 and Genie 3 extend the interactive generated-environment direction. The official Genie 3 report describes 720p generation at 24 fps and consistency over minutes. Such demonstrations are relevant to controllability, persistence, and user interaction. They do not measure an autonomous robot's transfer success. A model can produce coherent-looking landscapes while still permitting impossible topology changes or inventing contact outcomes. The distinction is a demand for the evaluation appropriate to the intended use. [18] [19]

9.2 V-JEPA 2: predict what a representation preserves

A joint-embedding predictive architecture predicts target encoder features from partially observed context instead of reconstructing raw pixels. A target encoder with an appropriate training rule supplies the desired embeddings; masking forces the predictor to infer structure beyond the visible input. Predicting in representation space can avoid spending capacity on unpredictable low-level appearance. The cost is that the encoder decides what information remains available to the world model. [20]

V-JEPA 2 first learns from large-scale video and image data. Its action-conditioned post-training freezes the video encoder and trains a causal predictor over visual features, robot state, and action tokens. An action-free masked-video objective teaches visual structure; it does not by itself identify a controlled transition function. The post-training stage supplies the missing intervention interface.

zt=frozen_encoder⁡(ot),z^t+1=predictor⁡(z≤t,state≤t,action≤t),LTF=∑t∥z^t+1−zt+1∥1,Lrollout=∥predictor_unrolled⁡(zt,at:t+H−1)−zt+H∥1,A∗=arg min⁡A∥predicted_goal_feature⁡(A)−encoder⁡(goal image)∥1.\begin{aligned}z_t&=\operatorname{frozen\_encoder}(o_t),\\\hat z_{t+1}&=\operatorname{predictor}(z_{\le t},\mathrm{state}_{\le t},\mathrm{action}_{\le t}),\\\mathcal L_{\mathrm{TF}}&=\sum_t\|\hat z_{t+1}-z_{t+1}\|_1,\\\mathcal L_{\mathrm{rollout}}&=\|\operatorname{predictor\_unrolled}(z_t,a_{t:t+H-1})-z_{t+H}\|_1,\\A^*&=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_A\|\operatorname{predicted\_goal\_feature}(A)-\operatorname{encoder}(\mathrm{goal\ image})\|_1.\end{aligned}zt​z^t+1​LTF​Lrollout​A∗​=frozen_encoder(ot​),=predictor(z≤t​,state≤t​,action≤t​),=t∑​∥z^t+1​−zt+1​∥1​,=∥predictor_unrolled(zt​,at:t+H−1​)−zt+H​∥1​,=Aargmin​∥predicted_goal_feature(A)−encoder(goal image)∥1​.​

Original Figure 6 contrasts teacher forcing and recurrent rollout supervision. On the left, each next-feature prediction receives the true feature from the previous frame. On the right, predictions become subsequent inputs. The encoder stays frozen in both. The drawn multi-step diagram is illustrative; the method section specifies a two-step rollout loss in the actual training recipe. This is the same structural problem as PlaNet's overshooting, now in a different representation: accurate one-step predictions conditioned on truth do not ensure stable free-running prediction.

A crucial terminology detail is easy to miss. The paper calls the robot videos “unlabeled” because task names, reward, and success labels are not used. It does use robot state metadata and constructs actions from changes in end-effector state. The post-training subset is under 62 hours; the selected clips are sampled at 4 fps. This is not a model that learned calibrated robot control solely by watching anonymous internet video. Action/state conventions supply the grounding that passive observation cannot identify on its own.

Original Figure 7 implements goal reaching as feature-energy minimization. Encode the current view and goal image, roll candidate actions through the predictor, compare the terminal feature to the goal, and optimize actions with CEM.
