Execute only the first action and repeat. The dashed red distance is an optimization objective, not a measured physical distance in meters. Its usefulness depends on the learned representation ranking physically successful states ahead of visually similar failures.

This leads to concrete tests. Does the energy decrease when the gripper approaches the correct object rather than merely producing a similar silhouette? Is it invariant to nuisance camera exposure while remaining sensitive to object contact? Can it distinguish “object inside closed drawer” from “object behind drawer in the image”? If several physical states map to nearby features but require different actions, planning can converge to the wrong one despite an excellent feature prediction loss.

9.3 Cosmos and the difference between a platform and a controller

Cosmos provides data curation, tokenization, pretrained generative models, and adaptation tools for physical-AI workloads. Such a platform can support scenario generation, visual augmentation, and specialized predictors. It should be evaluated at the level of the customized task: are generated trajectories temporally consistent, are control labels valid, and does downstream performance improve on held-out real conditions? A foundation-model label does not supply these guarantees. [21]

The broader lesson from APV, Genie, and V-JEPA 2 is that abundant passive video and scarce intervention data are complementary. Video teaches appearance, motion regularities, objects, and scene structure. Intervention data anchors controllable variables, timing, and action consequences. Their combination can reduce the amount of robot data needed, but missing action coverage remains a source of uncertainty. This is why world-model development and robotics data collection cannot be understood independently.

10 · Dreamer 4: scalable generation must be fast enough for policy improvement

Dreamer 4 changes both the model and the data regime. It trains a causal video tokenizer and an interactive generative dynamics Transformer, then learns behavior through offline imagination. Unlike DreamerV3's online exploration setting, its Minecraft diamond challenge forbids environment interaction during agent learning. The model must therefore be good enough to support improvement without repeatedly correcting its mistakes through new real rollouts. [8]

10.1 Architecture: frame-causal compression and selective temporal attention

Original Figure 2 shows the tokenizer on the left and dynamics on the right. The tokenizer compresses image patches into continuous latent tokens through a bounded bottleneck and reconstructs them with a causal decoder. The dynamics sequence interleaves action information, noise/step-size information, and noisy latent representations. Spatial layers mix information within a frame; causal temporal layers bring in history. The distinction matters because interactive simulation must generate the next frame before receiving the next user or policy action; a noncausal video encoder that requires future frames would violate that contract.

The dynamics architecture uses temporal attention only periodically among spatial layers and applies grouped-query attention to reduce KV-cache traffic. Thus the model directly connects to the LLM serving topics in this library: a long world-model context is also a growing attention-memory problem. More spatial tokens improve detail, while more temporal tokens preserve history. Both consume memory and compute. Reporting only parameter count hides these separate scaling axes.

10.2 Shortcut forcing: two time axes and a bounded inference budget

Let t denote environment time and τ the signal level of a corrupted latent. Mix noise z_0 with data latent z_1 to form zτ=(1−τ)z0+τz1z_\tau=(1-\tau)z_0+\tau z_1zτ​=(1−τ)z0​+τz1​. The model is conditioned on both τ and the requested integration step size d. At the smallest step size it learns from data; at larger step sizes it learns a consistency target constructed from shorter steps. This combines shortcut-style few-step generation with a sequence objective that sees different corruption levels over time.

zτ=(1−τ)znoise+τzdata,z^data=fθ(zτ,τ,d,action/context),Small-step target:observed clean latent,Large-step target:stop-gradient composition of two shorter predictions,Inference:K=4 updates per new frame (reported).\begin{aligned}z_\tau&=(1-\tau)z_{\mathrm{noise}}+\tau z_{\mathrm{data}},\\\hat z_{\mathrm{data}}&=f_\theta(z_\tau,\tau,d,\mathrm{action/context}),\\\text{Small-step target:}&\quad\text{observed clean latent},\\\text{Large-step target:}&\quad\text{stop-gradient composition of two shorter predictions},\\\text{Inference:}&\quad K=4\text{ updates per new frame (reported)}.\end{aligned}zτ​z^data​Small-step target:Large-step target:Inference:​=(1−τ)znoise​+τzdata​,=fθ​(zτ​,τ,d,action/context),observed clean latent,stop-gradient composition of two shorter predictions,K=4 updates per new frame (reported).​

The paper parameterizes the network in clean-data space rather than directly using a high-frequency velocity output for all objectives. Its argument is about accumulated error during sequential generation: an output parameterization that works for one isolated sample can behave differently when samples recursively condition future samples. Ramp weighting changes which signal levels receive the most learning emphasis. These choices aim to keep fast rollouts stable, because an imagination learner cannot afford an image-generation-grade sampling budget at every step.

This abbreviated formulation explains the mechanism without obscuring the distinction between environment horizon and integration steps. Increasing K improves the numerical/generative step but multiplies transition cost. Increasing context preserves longer environmental history but expands attention work. Neither is the same as increasing the actor's imagination horizon. All three should be exposed in a reproducible benchmark configuration.

Derivation: a long generative step can be supervised by two shorter steps

Let τ denote generative noise time, not environment time. A step-size-conditioned vector field v(x,τ,h) defines a macro-update x′=x+h v(x,τ,h). Assume the admissible interval contains τ+2h. Execute two h-steps and compare them with one 2h-step:

v1=v(x,τ,h),xmid=x+hv1,v2=v(xmid,τ+h,h),xend=xmid+hv2=x+h(v1+v2),xlong=x+2h v(x,τ,2h),Endpoint matching:v(x,τ,2h)=12(v1+v2).\begin{aligned}v_1&=v(x,\tau,h),&x_{\mathrm{mid}}&=x+hv_1,\\v_2&=v(x_{\mathrm{mid}},\tau+h,h),&x_{\mathrm{end}}&=x_{\mathrm{mid}}+hv_2\\&&&=x+h(v_1+v_2),\\x_{\mathrm{long}}&=x+2h\,v(x,\tau,2h),\\\text{Endpoint matching:}\quad v(x,\tau,2h)&=\tfrac12(v_1+v_2).\end{aligned}v1​v2​xlong​Endpoint matching:v(x,τ,2h)​=v(x,τ,h),=v(xmid​,τ+h,h),=x+2hv(x,τ,2h),=21​(v1​+v2​).​xmid​xend​​=x+hv1​,=xmid​+hv2​=x+h(v1​+v2​),​

The factor one-half is forced by equal displacement over a doubled interval. A training target can evaluate the two shorter predictions, stop their gradients, and train the larger-step prediction toward their average. Repeating this over a hierarchy of step sizes teaches fewer-call generation while retaining a connection to shorter-step behavior. The target depends on the midpoint reached after the first step; averaging two velocities at the original x would represent a different approximation.

What this does not prove. Self-consistency is not correctness. A field that consistently generates the wrong future can satisfy its own shortcut targets. Grounding at small steps in real training data and evaluating generated trajectories remain necessary. Nor does halving the number of denoiser calls necessarily halve total simulator time: tokenization, temporal attention, cache movement, and policy/value heads remain. Dreamer 4 combines this kind of generative consistency with causal sequence modeling and behavioral learning; their clocks and gradient paths should be tracked separately.

10.3 Task conditioning must not leak into the predicted physics

The model inserts task-conditioned agent tokens that can read the world representation and predict actions, rewards, and values. Other modalities do not attend back to the agent tokens. This asymmetric mask prevents a requested task from directly altering the model's environmental predictions. The policy can change the world through its actions; “please obtain a diamond” must not make the simulator hallucinate one independently of those actions.

After behavioral initialization, imagination training freezes the main Transformer and updates policy and value heads. A frozen behavioral prior constrains policy drift. The policy objective uses PMPO, which separates positive- and negative-advantage samples and uses their sign rather than raw magnitude. This avoids allowing tasks with large numerical return scales to dominate the update. A KL to the behavioral prior keeps the learned policy near plausible action behavior; it reduces some exploitation opportunities without proving the simulator correct.

Original Figure 3 plots successive Minecraft milestones under the offline challenge. Each group is an item, and the vertical axis is the fraction of episodes obtaining it. Early easy items can have similar high success across agents while late milestones separate them sharply. The linked paper reports 29% iron-pickaxe success and 0.7% diamond success for Dreamer 4 in this experiment. The diamond result establishes that the offline pipeline can produce the behavior; its small success fraction also shows the distance from reliable completion. “Obtains diamonds” should not be read as “solves every run.”

The paper separately tests human interaction inside the simulator on 16 tasks, reporting 14 successful tasks for Dreamer 4, and measures around 21 generated frames per second for its 2B model on one H100 in the stated configuration. That is a different evaluation from autonomous diamond acquisition. One tests modeled game mechanics under human control; the other tests policy improvement and long-horizon autonomous execution. Keeping them separate clarifies what a better generative model has actually enabled.

11 · Error analysis: prediction quality becomes control quality only through a chain of assumptions

11.1 A simple rollout-error bound, and its limitations

Assume a deterministic transition approximation has one-step error at most ε on the states and actions reached, and the true dynamics are L-Lipschitz under the same action sequence. Starting from the same state, the error recursion is:

et+1≤Let+ε,eH≤ε∑i=0H−1Li={Hε,L=1,εLH−1L−1,L≠1.\begin{aligned}e_{t+1}&\le Le_t+\varepsilon,\\e_H&\le\varepsilon\sum_{i=0}^{H-1}L^i=\begin{cases}H\varepsilon,&L=1,\\\displaystyle\varepsilon\frac{L^H-1}{L-1},&L\ne1.\end{cases}\end{aligned}et+1​eH​​≤Let​+ε,≤εi=0∑H−1​Li=⎩⎨⎧​Hε,εL−1LH−1​,​L=1,L=1.​​

Illustrative bound ε Σ L^i with matching actions and zero initial error. It ignores stochastic distributions and policy feedback; use it to understand why horizon matters.

The assumption that the error bound holds on reached states is doing real work. A low average validation loss on the dataset does not imply it. An optimizing policy can leave that support. Contact events can violate a useful smoothness constant, and hidden-state ambiguity requires distributional reasoning. If the policy itself responds to erroneous predicted state, its sensitivity also enters the closed-loop recursion. This calculator is a teaching bound, not a prediction of any model's benchmark performance.

11.2 Value errors matter in directions selected by the policy

Suppose rewards differ by at most ε_r and transition distributions have total-variation error ε_P uniformly over a relevant state–action set. With bounded rewards and a fixed policy, a standard simulation-lemma-style argument produces value error terms scaling like εr1−γ\frac{\varepsilon_r}{1-\gamma}1−γεr​​ and γRmax⁡εP(1−γ)2\frac{\gamma R_{\max}\varepsilon_P}{(1-\gamma)^2}(1−γ)2γRmax​εP​​, with constants depending on the total-variation convention. Long effective horizons magnify transition errors. The useful lesson is the dependence on horizon and support, not a universal numerical guarantee for a neural model.

A global pixel error is usually a poor proxy for this value error. Missing a reward-triggering collision can be much worse than a large background texture mismatch. Yet weighting only current reward can remove information needed for future tasks. The field repeatedly moves between broad reconstruction supervision and task-oriented abstraction because neither objective alone solves both sample efficiency and reuse.

Derivation: a precise transition-error bound and the price of optimizing the model

Assumptions. Compare two MDPs with discount 0≤γ<1 on the same state/action space. Their rewards lie in [0,Rmax], differ by at most εr, and their next-state distributions differ uniformly by at most εP in total variation TV(P,Q)=½∥P−Q∥₁. Fix a policy π. These are strong uniform assumptions over all relevant state-action pairs, not consequences of a low mean pixel error.

Let Δ=∥Vπ−V̂π∥∞. Subtract the two Bellman equations, adding and subtracting γPπV̂π. A Markov operator does not increase sup norm, and for f in [0,M], |E_Pf−E_Qf|≤M TV(P,Q). Since V̂π∈[0,Rmax/(1−γ)]:

Vπ−V^π=(rπ−r^π)+γPπ(Vπ−V^π)+γ(Pπ−P^π)V^π,Δ≤εr+γΔ+γεPRmax⁡1−γ,Δ≤εr1−γ+γRmax⁡εP(1−γ)2≡δ.\begin{aligned}V^\pi-\hat V^\pi&=(r^\pi-\hat r^\pi)+\gamma P^\pi(V^\pi-\hat V^\pi)\\&\quad+\gamma(P^\pi-\hat P^\pi)\hat V^\pi,\\\Delta&\le\varepsilon_r+\gamma\Delta+\frac{\gamma\varepsilon_PR_{\max}}{1-\gamma},\\\Delta&\le\frac{\varepsilon_r}{1-\gamma}+\frac{\gamma R_{\max}\varepsilon_P}{(1-\gamma)^2}\equiv\delta.\end{aligned}Vπ−V^πΔΔ​=(rπ−r^π)+γPπ(Vπ−V^π)+γ(Pπ−P^π)V^π,≤εr​+γΔ+1−γγεP​Rmax​​,≤1−γεr​​+(1−γ)2γRmax​εP​​≡δ.​

The first denominator sums direct reward errors over time. The second squared denominator accounts for both accumulated transition mismatch and the remaining future return affected by each mismatch. If rewards instead lie in [−Rmax,Rmax], using the value range gives a factor two in the transition term under this TV convention. Stating the reward range and the convention removes that otherwise ambiguous constant.

If the same bound holds for every candidate policy, and π̂ maximizes model return, the true optimality gap satisfies J(π*)−J(π̂)≤2δ by the same add-and-subtract argument as the MPC ranking bound. An η-suboptimal model planner gives 2δ+η. A stronger optimizer cannot rescue a bound that fails outside the data support.

For deterministic closed-loop state error, policy sensitivity enters too. If f is Lx-Lipschitz in state, La-Lipschitz in action, and π is Lπ-Lipschitz, then eₜ₊₁≤(Lx+LaLπ)eₜ+ε. The familiar fixed-action factor Lx alone is insufficient when erroneous states also change actions. Contact discontinuities or an argmax policy can invalidate a useful finite Lipschitz constant.

Assume γ=0.9, Rmax=1, εr=0.01, and εP=0.005 under the stated nonnegative-reward/TV convention. Compute the fixed-policy value bound and exact-model-planning regret bound. Then halve εP and identify the contribution that remains.

The reward-error term remains 0.1. A bound larger than a measured gap does not contradict the experiment; this worst-case analysis lets all errors align adversarially over the horizon. Conversely, a small observed average transition error does not license substituting it for the uniform εP. The proof would need an occupancy-weighted or coverage-aware refinement for that setting.

11.3 Model exploitation is an optimization phenomenon

Consider two plans: one has true return 8 and predicted return 8; another has true return 1 but predicted return 12 because the model allows passing through a wall. A stronger optimizer selects the second plan more reliably. Better search can therefore reduce real performance. Increasing ensemble size helps only if disagreement detects the invalid trajectory. A value critic trained inside the same flawed simulator may reinforce the error instead of correcting it.

Useful countermeasures act at different places: gather intervention data around the exploited region, shorten rollouts, replan frequently, penalize uncertainty, constrain actions to supported behavior, or validate candidate plans with a separate model or physical constraint. Each has a cost. Pessimism can reject an effective but rare strategy; a behavioral prior can prevent improvement beyond demonstrations; short horizons can miss long-term consequences. A paper's gain should be interpreted through which failure it reduces and which capability it sacrifices.

11.4 Causality, confounding, and information leaks

Passive observational data can confound action and scene context. If a human always opens a cupboard when a particular object is present, a model may use the object as a shortcut for the cupboard transition. Intervening with a different action breaks that correlation. Action-conditioned likelihood is necessary but insufficient for causal identification when unobserved variables influence both actions and outcomes.

Evaluation should hold the initial state fixed and vary actions, including counterfactual actions absent from ordinary demonstration trajectories. Check action sensitivity, invariances, and timing. Also audit data leakage: an inverse-dynamics encoder may see the next frame while an online policy cannot; a video tokenizer may be noncausal; a reward head may indirectly receive future task labels. Such information can improve offline metrics while making the deployed control loop impossible.

12 · The systems cost of imagination

A world model creates value when its synthetic experience is cheaper or more informative than the real alternative. The correct denominator is not just model FLOPs. Include encoding, decoding, sequential sampling, KV-cache reads, reward inference, policy/value inference, replay movement, and synchronization. On physical robots, reset time, wear, human supervision, and risk can dominate; in a fast simulator, neural imagination may actually be slower than stepping the true engine.

FamilyTypical sequential work per imagined transitionMain online costMain scaling pressure
RSSM latent actorRecurrent transition and small headsEncode observation + actorReplay ratio, latent width, number of imagined trajectories
CEM / MPPI latent plannerPopulation × horizon model evaluationsPlanning iterations on every decisionCandidate count, horizon, action dimension
MuZero-style searchDynamics/prediction per expanded nodeSearch simulationsBranching factor, tree depth, accelerator batching
Autoregressive image-token modelK visual-token generations per frameSimulator rollout or trained actorToken count and attention context
Diffusion / flow simulatorK denoising/flow evaluations per frameGeneration or trained actorSampling steps, resolution, context, cache traffic
Embedding predictorFeature transition, often several rollout stepsCandidate planning and feature-distance evaluationFeature-map size and planning population

For a planner with population P, horizon H, and I optimizer iterations, transition work is roughly IPHIPHIPH model calls before reuse or parallelization. A population can be batched, but temporal recurrence still serializes H steps. Batched throughput and decision latency are therefore different metrics. A system that imagines thousands of trajectories per second can still miss a robot's next control deadline.

For a token simulator with K codes per frame and H frames, naive autoregression requires roughly KH sequential prediction positions. For a diffusion simulator with S denoising evaluations per frame, the corresponding factor is SH, but each call may process an entire frame. Counting “steps” without the width and cost of each step is misleading. Architecture comparisons should report achieved transitions per second at a specified resolution, context, batch size, and hardware, plus policy performance using that budget.

The tabulated values are reproduced as reported, not independently rerun. Numbers with different observation modalities, resets, action repeats, hardware, or pretraining budgets must not be collapsed into a leaderboard. Atari 100k counts environment interactions under a particular protocol; an internet-pretrained model with the same online step count has consumed a different information budget.

13.2 The five evaluations a useful world model should survive

Representation test: does the encoder preserve small task-relevant objects, velocity cues, and occluded-state information? Compare reconstruction or feature behavior under carefully chosen perturbations. An easy downstream classifier can conceal a missing contact state.

Teacher-forced prediction test: given a true history and recorded action, how well does the model predict the next reward, termination, state, or observation? Measure calibration as well as average error. This isolates local prediction but understates deployment drift.

Free-running and counterfactual test: condition on a prefix, roll out without future observations, and vary the action sequence. Evaluate event timing, object persistence, action sensitivity, and rare transitions. Plausible alternative futures should not be penalized as if a stochastic process were deterministic, but impossible outcomes should be.

Decision-ranking test: compare the model's ranking of candidate actions or plans with real-environment returns. Rank correlation or pairwise preference accuracy can be more relevant than a perceptual metric. Include candidates selected by an optimizer, because random candidates may never expose exploitable errors.

Closed-loop policy test: deploy the planner or imagined policy in the real environment and measure return, success, intervention rate, and latency. Report seeds, confidence intervals, resets, and failure categories. Good offline prediction plus poor real control is evidence that some part of the model-use chain is wrong, not merely an inconvenient benchmark result.

For aggregate RL scores, include median, interquartile mean, performance profiles, and per-task results rather than only the arithmetic mean. The human-normalized Atari score agent−randomhuman−random\frac{\mathrm{agent}-\mathrm{random}}{\mathrm{human}-\mathrm{random}}human−randomagent−random​ can become very large on individual games. A higher mean can coexist with weaker typical-game performance. Scientific interpretation requires seeing that distribution.

14 · Choosing a model, designing experiments, and the open problems

14.1 Choose the model by the missing capability

If physical interaction is expensive and state is low dimensional, probabilistic dynamics with uncertainty-aware MPC offers a direct path from data to control. If the task is visual RL and action-time latency is tight, latent imagination with an actor is attractive. If the goal changes and online computation is available, a planner can adapt its objective without retraining the whole actor, provided the model retains the needed state distinctions.

If small visual details govern reward, test whether the latent bottleneck preserves them before scaling the controller. If broad passive-video pretraining is available, plan an explicit action-grounding stage and validate intervention coverage. If the objective is synthetic-data generation, evaluate the downstream policy trained on those samples; visual diversity is valuable only when the labels and physical consequences remain usable.

Observed failureCandidate causeExperiment that separates it
Sharp reconstructions, drifting imagined futuresPosterior/prior gap or exposure biasPrefix-conditioned free rollout; compare one-step and recurrent loss
High predicted return, low real returnModel exploitation or reward hallucinationExecute top-ranked and random plans; inspect uncertainty and constraints
Good easy tasks, poor new rewardTask-oriented state discarded required informationChange only reward or goal while holding visual dynamics fixed
Good video metrics, wrong action consequencesConfounding or weak action conditioningFixed-start counterfactual action sweeps
Large model, no training benefitOptimization instability or data bottleneckScale with fixed data and fixed compute separately; monitor gradient/target scales
Good simulator, weak agentInsufficient exploration, critic error, policy optimizationCompare expert/human control, MPC, and learned actor in the same model
Good offline score, missed real-time deadlinesHidden sequential generation/planning costEnd-to-end latency under deployed batch/context settings

14.2 Open problems with concrete research questions

Action-conditioned generalization: can a model trained on one embodiment identify reusable consequences rather than memorizing its actuator convention? Test transfer across control frequency, geometry, and contact conditions with the interface explicitly calibrated.

Long-horizon state: how can a simulator preserve an object or irreversible event beyond a finite visual context? A larger KV cache is one solution, but persistent structured memory and state estimation may be more efficient. Evaluate revisiting a changed scene after a long detour.

Calibrated model trust: can uncertainty predict which candidate plan will fail in reality, after the planner has optimized against it? This is stronger than calibration on randomly held-out transitions. It demands evaluation under selection.

Reusable abstraction: can a latent ignore visual nuisance while preserving variables relevant to a family of future rewards? Reconstruction, predictive embeddings, and value equivalence occupy different points in this tradeoff. A meaningful benchmark should vary downstream goals, not only initial states.

Offline improvement without simulator exploitation: behavioral priors and conservative objectives help, but their conservatism can cap performance. A robust system should identify when imagined improvement is supported by data and when new intervention data is required. That decision is an active-learning and deployment problem as well as an RL algorithm.

14.3 Reading route and derivation exercises

Read PETS → PlaNet → Dreamer to understand the uncertainty, representation, and computation transitions. Then read DreamerV2/V3 with their ablations, and MuZero → EfficientZero → TD-MPC2 as the decision-oriented branch. Read IRIS → DIAMOND for the observation-fidelity argument, followed by Genie → V-JEPA 2 → Dreamer 4 for the transition from passive video to grounded policy learning.

Derive the RSSM ELBO and identify every place where a future observation is allowed during training but unavailable at inference. Reimplement the KL-balancing expression and check which network receives each gradient. Construct a two-mode transition where a conditional-mean predictor leads to an impossible state. Compare a short-horizon MPC and an actor trained inside the same model at equal real data and equal total accelerator time. Finally, design an experiment where better video likelihood worsens action ranking, then identify which representation or objective change would address that failure.

The lasting knowledge is a method of interrogation: what does the model preserve, which interventions ground it, what optimization will exploit it, and which real-world measurement verifies its usefulness? Every architecture in this guide should be understood through those four questions.
